sentences.text: Patagotitan was a massive quadrupedal herbivore distinguished by an exceptionally long neck and tail.
Scientists distinguish this species from close relatives by unique anatomical features found in its back and tail vertebrae, shoulder blades, forelimb bones, and hindlimb bones.

The genus Patagotitan was formally described by Carballido and colleagues in 2017. It is a titanosaurian sauropod from the Early Cretaceous Albian stage of the Cerro Barcino Formation in Chubut Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
The initial discovery involved a partial lower femur found in 2010 by farm laborer Aurelio Hernández near La Flecha, approximately 250 km west of Trelew.
Subsequent excavations uncovered more than 200 fossils, comprising 130 sauropod bones and 57 theropod teeth.

Patagotitan lived in a forested floodplain environment dominated by coniferous trees, where angiosperms were rare. A new genus of cypress, Austrocupressinoxylon, was named in 2019 from fossil wood found near the site.
Patagotitan belongs to the clade Lognkosauria and is characterized as a large and robust titanosaur.
A 2017 analysis placed Patagotitan as the sister group to Argentinosaurus.
Carballido and colleagues later used Patagotitan in 2022 to help redefine the group Colossosauria.
This animal lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 101 million years ago in the Cenomanian, in what is now South America.

Preliminary estimates suggested Patagotitan reached a length of 37 meters and a weight of 69 tonnes, though these figures were later revised to approximately 31 meters in length and 50 to 60 tonnes in weight.

There is a debate regarding Patagotitan's maximum size, with initial estimates of 37 meters and 69 tonnes later revised down to 31 meters and 50-60 tonnes, placing it potentially smaller than Argentinosaurus and Puertasaurus. A 2014 news report estimated Patagotitan to be 40 meters long and weigh 77 tonnes, while Carballido and colleagues estimated its weight between 44.2 and 77.6 tonnes using volumetric methods in 2017. Science writer Riley Black and paleontologist Matt Wedel cautioned against these size estimates following the 2017 publication. Matt Wedel criticized the polygon-based method used to compare Patagotitan and Argentinosaurus vertebrae, noting the former was largely empty space. Gregory S. Paul argued in 2019 that Patagotitan could not have had a larger torso than Argentinosaurus because its articulated back vertebrae were shorter.
